title: Personal best marathon performance is associated with performance in a 24-h run and not anthropometry or training volume
authors: Knechtle B, Wirth A, Knechtle P, Zimmermann K, Kohler G
population: 15 male Caucasian ultra-runners (mean age 46.7 years) in a 24-h run
findings: No significant association (p>0.05) between distance reached and anthropometry, weekly training hours, running years, number of finished marathons or 24-h runs.
Distance reached correlated with personal best marathon time (r2 = 0.40, p<0.05) and personal best 24-h distance (r2 = 0.58, p<0.05).
Personal best marathon time correlated with personal best 24-h distance (r2 = 0.76, p<0.01).
Authors conclude training volume does not appear to have a major effect and a fast personal best marathon time was the only positive association.
limitations: n=15, self-reported, narrow range of volume among experienced ultra-runners, underpowered; a null result is not evidence of no effect. Crossref 2008 online vs Europe PMC 2009 issue.
implications: Use a proven race-speed capacity (recent marathon or half time) as an input beside volume when judging 100 km to 24 h feasibility.
No change to volume rules is justified; use it to widen ultra uncertainty intervals.

verification.notes: Crossref title, journal, first author match; year 2009 (issue) kept. Abstract re-fetched, numbers match. Evidence downgrade not needed; level C is generous for n=15 and is treated as D-weight in rules.
